title: HubSpot AEO vs. Otterly: Platform or standalone tool?
content:
Here’s the question most teams are actually trying to answer: do you need a standalone tool to monitor how your brand shows up in AI search, or do you need something that connects that monitoring to the content and CRM workflows that let you act on it?
That’s the real difference between HubSpot AEO and Otterly. Both track your visibility in AI engines like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. But what happens after the data comes in is where they diverge.
HubSpot AEO is a CRM-connected AEO solution built directly into the HubSpot platform. It surfaces visibility insights and routes them into content creation, campaign management, and pipeline tracking, without requiring you to switch tools. Otterly is a standalone AEO monitoring tool that tracks your AI visibility, provides reporting, and lets you export data via Looker Studio, an API, or an MCP server.
If you’re trying to decide between them, here’s an honest breakdown.
HubSpot AEO is built into the HubSpot platform. It tracks how your brand appears across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, then connects those insights directly to your CRM data, marketing campaigns, and content tools.
When it surfaces a gap, you can publish a blog post, schedule a LinkedIn update, or engage on Reddit without leaving HubSpot. The prompt suggestions it gives you aren’t generic industry templates — they’re built from what it already knows about your company, competitors, and customers.
Otterly is a purpose-built content intelligence platform for AI search. It calls itself “neutral and objective,” tracking from a first-person perspective on a daily basis. It covers a wider range of AI engines out of the box (ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, Perplexity, and Microsoft Copilot), with Google Gemini and Claude available as paid add-ons.
Otterly offers strong standalone reporting and integrates with Looker Studio, a public API, and an MCP server. What it doesn’t do is connect that data to a CRM, marketing automation, or content creation workflow — that part is up to you.
The core decision lens: if your team just needs AI visibility monitoring and has a separate content workflow you’re happy with, Otterly works. If you want AEO insights to flow directly into the tools where you create content, run campaigns, and track pipeline, HubSpot AEO is the stronger fit.
Here’s a side-by-side look at what each tool actually does:
ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot (Gemini + Claude as add-ons)
This is where the two tools take meaningfully different approaches.
HubSpot AEO uses your CRM data to suggest prompts from the start. Because it knows your industry, competitors, and customer profile, the prompts it recommends tend to reflect actual buyer questions rather than generic category queries. You still pick the final set, but you’re not starting from a blank page.
Otterly’s Query Fan Out Tool takes a different approach: you give it a single user prompt, and it shows the full range of related queries an AI engine might generate from that starting point. This is useful for prompt discovery and gap analysis, especially if you’re building a prompt library from scratch or want to understand how far a topic branches.
For citation tracking, Otterly monitors domain citations and specific URLs weekly. HubSpot tracks which domains, pages, and content types are being cited in AI answers for your category, and lets you filter by source type (owned, competitor, third-party, social, affiliate) and content type (blog, news, product, social).
Pro tip: If you’re a HubSpot user, the prompt suggestions that come from your CRM data save real setup time.
HubSpot AEO transforms visibility gaps into prioritized recommendations. You don’t have to interpret a dashboard and figure out what to do next — it tells you.
Otterly gives you a Content Audit with a predictive GEO score and actionable optimization tips, plus a Crawlability Checker to confirm AI bots can actually read your site. Those are useful diagnostic tools that HubSpot AEO doesn’t offer. But they stop at the recommendation level — executing on them happens outside Otterly.
This is the clearest difference between the two tools.
With HubSpot AEO and Marketing Hub, when the data shows your brand isn’t showing up for a key prompt, you can write a blog post, schedule a social update, or engage on a third-party platform without leaving HubSpot. Your AEO data and campaign metrics live in the same place, so you can connect a visibility shift to the content that drove it.
With Otterly, you get the insight, go to your content tool, publish, then come back to Otterly later to see if it moved the needle. For some teams that workflow is fine. For others, the context-switching slows things down.
Best for workflow efficiency: HubSpot AEO, if your team already uses HubSpot for content or marketing. Otterly, if you want a monitoring layer that sits on top of your existing stack without changing how you work.
If you’re already using HubSpot’s Marketing Hub or Content Hub, AEO data can connect directly to your automation workflows. When you publish content to close a visibility gap, you can trigger nurture sequences, update contact properties, or route leads based on what they were searching for in AI. That’s not a feature of AEO alone — it’s what happens when AEO lives inside a platform with CRM and automation already built in.
Otterly doesn’t offer this. It’s a monitoring and reporting tool, not a marketing automation platform. If you need to connect AEO insights to lead nurturing, you’d use Otterly’s API to pull data into whatever system you use for that. For more on how generative engine optimization fits into this picture, that’s worth reading alongside your tooling decision.
HubSpot AEO is available as a standalone tool at $50/month (or $45/month billed annually). The free trial runs 28 days and includes 25 prompts across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity — no credit card required.
If you want AEO built into your full marketing and content platform, HubSpot for Marketers (Marketing Hub + Content Hub + AEO) starts at $900/month.
Otterly offers a 7-day free trial, then three paid tiers:
Note that Otterly’s base plans don’t include Gemini or Claude tracking — those are add-ons. If you need coverage across all major engines, factor add-on costs into your total.
Otterly also offers an Agency Partner tier on Standard or Premium plans, which increases prompt limits (150 for Standard, 500 for Premium), adds unlimited workspace management, and includes white-labeled Looker Studio reports at no extra charge.
What this means in practice: For a small team that just needs to monitor 15 or fewer prompts across major AI engines, Otterly Lite at $29/month covers the basics. For a team that wants CRM-connected visibility and doesn’t need a high prompt volume, HubSpot AEO at $50/month includes the workflow integration that Otterly doesn’t offer at any tier. For teams that need 100+ prompts, URL auditing, and API access, Otterly Standard at $189/month adds depth that the standalone HubSpot AEO plan doesn’t match — though you’d be managing those insights in a separate workflow.
If you’re already in HubSpot, AEO is the obvious fit because the integration is native. AEO data sits alongside your campaign metrics, contact records, and content performance in one place. When a visibility shift happens, you can trace it to a campaign, a piece of content, or a change in competitor presence without exporting to a spreadsheet.
Otterly’s integrations go in a different direction. Looker Studio lets you build custom dashboards. The public API lets you pipe data into your BI stack. The MCP server lets you query your AI visibility data in plain language from inside tools like Claude or Cursor. For teams with strong data infrastructure and a preference for custom reporting, Otterly’s integration approach gives more flexibility.
What we like about HubSpot AEO: You don’t have to build a reporting layer. The insights live where decisions get made.
This is where HubSpot AEO has a structural advantage. Because it’s CRM-connected, you can tie AI visibility to actual pipeline. If leads coming from AI search are converting faster (and HubSpot’s own data shows leads from AI convert at 3x the rate of traditional search), you can see that in the same system where your sales team is working those deals.
That kind of competitive intelligence loop, where you can see both where competitors are showing up in AI answers and how it’s affecting your own pipeline, is hard to build when your AEO tool and CRM are separate.
Otterly doesn’t have CRM connectivity. If you want to connect visibility data to sales outcomes, you’d need to pipe data out via API and join it in another tool.
Short answer: yes, they work together rather than replacing each other.
SEO optimizes for traditional search engine rankings — crawlability, keywords, backlinks, structured data. AEO optimizes for how your brand appears in AI-generated answers . The same page can rank well on Google and get cited in ChatGPT, or it can do one without the other.
What matters is that the content strategies overlap. A well-structured, authoritative piece of content is more likely to get cited in AI answers AND rank in traditional search. Writing for AI search emphasizes clear answers, first-person source authority, and structured data — all of which also support SEO fundamentals.
The practical way to connect the two: use your AEO prompt data to identify what buyers are asking AI, then check whether you have content that answers those questions clearly and in a format AI can cite. Gaps in your AEO visibility are often the same gaps as in your organic content strategy.
With HubSpot AEO, this loop is tighter because the recommendations tell you specifically which pages to create or update, and you can build them in Content Hub without changing tools. With Otterly, the Content Audit and GEO score point you to issues, and you handle the fix in your separate CMS.
Start small and specific. Most teams overcomplicate this by trying to track everything at once. Pick 10-15 prompts that map to the real questions your buyers ask when they’re evaluating solutions like yours. Think: “What’s the best [tool category] for [use case]?” and “How does [your product type] work?”
With HubSpot AEO, the tool will suggest prompts based on your CRM data, so you don’t have to start from scratch. With Otterly, the Query Fan Out Tool helps you expand a starting prompt into related queries your buyers might actually be using.
Either way, review your prompts every 30-60 days. Buyer questions evolve, and so do the answers AI engines give.
Monitoring makes sense when you’re just getting started and need to understand your baseline visibility before you commit to a content strategy. Otterly’s Lite tier at $29/month is a low-risk way to do that.
You should move toward a full platform when the data is telling you things you can’t act on fast enough. If you’re seeing visibility gaps but your team spends time switching between a monitoring tool, a content tool, and a CRM to close them, the context-switching is costing you more than the platform upgrade.
Pro tip: HubSpot’s 28-day free trial is long enough to establish a real visibility baseline and get your first round of recommendations without spending a dime. Start there before committing to either tool.
Otterly Lite at $29/month is the lower-cost entry point: 15 prompts, 4 AI engines, daily tracking, unlimited team members. HubSpot AEO at $50/month makes more sense if you’re already in HubSpot and want insights connected to your content and CRM workflows.
Yes. The $50/month standalone plan works with any CRM. CRM-connected features like personalized prompt suggestions and pipeline alignment require Marketing Hub Pro or Enterprise, but core visibility tracking, citations, and recommendations don’t.
Focus on evaluation-stage questions: “what’s the best [tool type] for [use case]” rather than broad category queries. Pull language from sales calls, support tickets, and customer interviews. HubSpot automatically suggests prompts from your CRM data; Otterly’s Query Fan Out Tool helps you expand a starting prompt into related queries.
Connect visibility to demand. HubSpot AEO with Marketing Hub lets you tie visibility changes to lead volume, conversion rates, and pipeline directly. Otterly’s Brand Visibility Index, Share of AI Voice, and sentiment data can be pulled into Looker Studio for custom reporting. Either way, if your score is rising but demand isn’t, revisit whether you’re tracking prompts that reflect real buyer intent.

title: Entity Mapping Works On Google. Does Any Of It Reach ChatGPT? via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester
content:
If entity mapping feels familiar, that is because you already ran this play. It is the knowledge graph conversation you were having in 2021, wearing a 2026 outfit. The vocabulary migrated almost intact: entities, not strings ; disambiguation; sameAs; relationships between nodes; feed the structure; and the machine understands you. Pull a client deck from four years ago, swap “Knowledge Graph” for “the AI,” and most of the slides would survive the move. That is why the term is spreading, and it is also the reason to slow down before you buy it. The compressed version, in case you read no further: entity mapping does real work on Google, where there is an actual graph to feed, and almost no work on the language model itself, where there is no graph to feed and never was. Those are two different systems with two different rules, and the industry sells them to you as one tactic. Keeping them apart is important for the systems and LLMs.
The Knowledge Graph is a real, curated object (not to be confused with, say, your knowledge graph, which is your own, maintained graph of entities and relationships). Google launched it in 2012 under the banner “ things, not strings ,” and it has spent the years since becoming the layer that decides who and what a query is about before a single result loads. You feed it, but only indirectly, through structured data , consistent third-party corroboration, and maybe a clean Wikidata entry that independent sources agree with. You do not fill out a form and submit yourself. You assemble enough agreement across the open web that Google’s systems conclude you are a distinct, real thing worth having a node for. The reason self-declaration alone does not do it is that the graph is a confidence machine, not a submission box. Your schema states what you claim to be; the node gets built and trusted when enough independent, credible sources say the same thing back to Google. That is why a well-referenced Wikidata item and a handful of authoritative mentions move more weight than a flawlessly marked-up page that only ever talks about itself, and it is why Google has spent recent years tightening the graph toward entities it can corroborate with confidence rather than ones that merely assert themselves. And because Google’s AI answers resolve entities against that same graph before they generate, the work now reaches past the 10 blue links and into the AI surfaces too. On Google, entity mapping has a target, and the target has a mailing address. This is the part the support crowd gets right, but there is more.
The conversation you had in 2021 assumed a discrete, inspectable, feedable object. A node you could pull up in a panel and correct when it was wrong. You could see your own entity, file a fix, and watch it change, and the whole practice grew up around a surface you could actually observe. Entity mapping keeps every word of that tactic and quietly repoints it at a system that has none of those properties. That repointing is the sleight of hand, and it works precisely because the words did not change. One assumption crosses the border undeclared: that the thing on the other side can be fed at all.
Start with the term, because the whole confusion lives in it. Parametric memory is the knowledge a model carries baked into its weights, learned once during training, and distinct from what it looks up live when it answers you. On the parametric side, there is no record of your brand to open and edit. No row, no node, no panel to correct. There is a diffuse statistical pattern smeared across billions of parameters, and it arrived there because the model read the corpus at scale, not because it read your markup. Interpretability researchers state it without hedging: Factual knowledge in these models is parametric and emergent , with no single parameter holding any given fact and recall arising instead from distributed activation across the network. The mechanism deserves to be stated precisely, because the imprecision is where the tactic hides. During training, the model sees your brand across millions of contexts and adjusts its weights to encode the statistical shape of how you are described: which entities you appear beside, which categories you fall into, which claims recur around you. Nothing in that process parses a schema block or honors a sameAs link. It reads language, at volume, and what survives is consensus, not code. Your page is one context among billions, and unless it is echoed and repeated elsewhere, its structured declarations weigh almost nothing against the mass of everything else the model ingested. You can add sameAs links until the whole page turns blue, and you will not have moved that pattern one inch, because the pattern never learned from your page. It learned from how often, how consistently, and how credibly the rest of the web talks about you. The uncomfortable consequence is that the highest-leverage entity work for the parametric side barely touches your website. It is getting cited in the places the model already trusts, earning mentions you do not control , and being described the same way by people who are not you. That work is slower, harder, and far more durable than a schema audit, which is exactly why the tidy on-site version outsells it.
Grant me, for the sake of argument, that you could somehow reach the parametric side and write to it. You still could not mirror your diagram onto it, because the thing you would be mirroring is not shaped like a diagram. It pays here to remember what entity mapping actually is underneath. Every structured data statement you make is a triple: a subject, a predicate, and an object. Your brand, sells, this product. This author, wrote, that article. That triple is the atomic unit of the semantic web, and it is the unit your entire entity practice exists to produce. It is also the unit the language model does not store. When researchers trace where this knowledge physically sits, they find that entity knowledge and relational knowledge live in different parts of the model and do not map onto each other . Change the entity in a fact and change the relationship in that same fact, and the model does not respond equivalently, even though your triple treats them as two interchangeable slots. So the clean subject-predicate-object structure your schema encodes, the very structure Google’s graph was built to consume, has no faithful counterpart inside the model at all. The nodes-and-edges picture-entity mapping draws is a human convenience, useful for planning and useless as a description of the model’s internals. There is no tidy graph in there waiting for you to align to, which makes the deliverable a map of a territory that was never organized as a map. That is not a tuning problem you fix with better markup. It is a category mismatch, and no amount of schema closes it. Practically, it means you should stop grading your parametric work by how complete your entity markup looks, because the tidiness of the map tells you nothing about whether the model holds the territory.
Picture a mid-market vendor that has done everything the playbook asks. Complete Organization schema, sameAs pointing at every profile, a clean internal entity graph across the whole site. Ask ChatGPT about its category with search enabled and the vendor turns up, because the fetch found those well-structured pages and lifted from them cleanly. Ask the identical question with search switched off and the vendor is simply absent, because the model’s training never saw enough of the world describe it to encode it at all. Same company, same markup, same platform, opposite outcomes, and the only thing that changed was whether the system was allowed to go read the page. Google’s own surfaces sit in a third position, resolving against the graph the vendor has been feeding all along, which is why that side of the work keeps looking like it is winning.
Do not let any of this collapse into “nothing-matters,” because that’s an over-reaction. AI search is not purely parametric, and retrieval is doing enormous work. It helps to separate the surfaces , since they behave differently. When a model answers from memory with no search, you are hitting the parametric side, and nothing on your page reaches it. When Perplexity, Google’s AI answers, or a model in search mode fetches live pages before responding, you are hitting the retrieval side, where clean structure and clear entity signals genuinely help you get pulled and quoted. Most real answers now blend the two, using parametric knowledge to frame the question and retrieval to fill in the specifics, and that blend is exactly why the tactic feels like it works: it moves the retrieval half, visibly, while doing nothing to the parametric half you cannot watch. Helping a retriever find you and parse you is not the same as the model having learned you. One is a door you can open this quarter with disambiguation and structure. The other is standing in the corpus that took years of being talked about to build and will take years to shift. Entity mapping reliably buys you the first and gets quietly sold to you as the second. Structured content earns you the fetch and a clean extraction; consistent corroboration across the wider web earns you the standing underneath it. Treating those as one item is the mistake.
This raises the obvious question of how you would ever know which system is actually moving. You cannot open the parametric side and inspect it, which is precisely what lets the promise go unchallenged. The only honest answer is to stop trusting the tactic’s story and watch the outputs directly : track whether you show up when the model answers from memory against when it answers from a live fetch, on the same questions, over time. If your presence climbs only on the retrieval-driven answers while the memory-only answers stay flat, you are watching the split happen in real time, and you are watching entity mapping do exactly half of what it was sold to do. Measurement is the tie-breaker the sales pitch cannot survive, which is the whole reason to insist on it.
You will see it written that your entity data now trains ChatGPT and Claude. It does not. Those models are not trained on Google’s proprietary graph, and the only reason the claim passes at a glance is that Gemini can use Google’s own graph, which lets a Google-specific truth borrow a universal costume. A second tell is subtler and more common. A vendor shows you that pages with rich schema get cited more often and calls it proof of causation. But that correlation is exactly what you would expect for an entirely different reason: the pages built carefully enough to carry complete markup tend to be the same pages that are well-sourced, well-linked, and widely referenced, which is what actually earns the citation. The schema rode along. It did not drive. Schema stays what it has always been, infrastructure that helps machines disambiguate you rather than a lever that pulls a citation, and anyone reporting a correlation between marked-up pages and citations is watching outputs, not reading a mechanism. So carry one question into every pitch you hear. Ask the person selling entity mapping to name the mechanism by which your on-site graph changes what the model learned during training. If the answer is that the schema helps the AI understand, you have been handed an observation dressed as a mechanism, and the price tag belongs to a different product. The literacy that separates the practitioners who will win from the ones running last year’s play is this: know which system you are actually feeding, and refuse to pay graph prices for parametric promises.
If you are running entity work right now and watching it move your Google presence while the LLM’s own answers stay put, that gap is the tell, and I would like to hear how it is showing up for you. Leave a comment below.
This post was originally published on Duane Forrester Decodes .
